BERT4Rec’s original paper explicitly acknowledges the mismatch between reconstructing interior masked items and predicting future interactions. Inference appends a reserved MASK token and reads its hidden state; training also includes examples masking only the final item to improve alignment. This aligns target placement and absence of right context, but does not establish matching context-length or endpoint distributions. Masking rate and maximum history length are dataset dependent; longer contexts do not consistently improve accuracy. [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690)

Implication for this experiment: terminal-MASK training on random prefixes provides partial alignment, not distributional equivalence. Uniformly sampled prefix endpoints include earlier interaction periods and often shorter histories than evaluation at each user’s latest boundary. Recency-sampling research supports treating target selection as consequential, although its reported applications do not directly validate a particular BERT4Rec prefix sampler. A reasonable hypothesis is to compare uniform prefixes with recent-endpoint sampling while matching inference truncation, padding and MASK placement. For a combined terminal and reconstruction objective, average each loss separately before applying its weight so long histories with more masked targets do not automatically dominate; this is an experimental design inference, not an established optimal weighting. Terminal placement alone also provides no guarantee against popularity bias: target frequencies and sampling remain relevant. Select sampling and auxiliary-loss weights using the fixed macro validation HR@10 within one jointly trained BERT4Rec per category. [Recency Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643)
